item.title: Evolution of Manhattan
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
From Lenape land to sprawling metropolis, this detailed timelapse animation captures the making of Manhattan

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: From the homeland of the Lenape people to a small Dutch colony to a battlefield of the American Revolution to the global cultural capital it’s become today, the island of Manhattan has undergone extraordinary transformations over the past several centuries. Rendered in 3D animation and created without the use of AI, this video from the YouTube channel City 3D Timelapse chronicles how this island of around just 22.7 square miles has evolved. It captures the spread of the population in the industrial era and, more recently, the reshaping of its skyline as supertall skyscrapers have gone up in rapid succession. The result is an extraordinary feat in its own right, condensing the making of modern Manhattan, in great detail and from several angles, into just eight minutes. For more from City 3D Timelapse, watch this video on the evolution of Paris.

item.title: The ghetto on the lagoon
item.dc:creator: Alexander Lee
item.description:
Sixteenth-century Venice wanted to expel its Jews but couldn’t do without them. Its compromise was the world’s first ghetto

- by Alexander Lee

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

25 minute listen

On 29 March 1516, the Venetian Senate voted to create the world’s first ‘ghetto’. All Jews then living in the city – as well as any others who might come later – were ordered to move immediately to a small island in the northeastern sestiere of Cannaregio, a neighbourhood known as the geto novo. It was anything but appealing. Previously used as a dumping ground for the communal copper foundry, it had been converted into a residential quarter for local workers. From the outside, it already looked ‘like a castle’ – ringed by canals and bounded by perilously tall tenements. But by the time Venice’s Jews were herded in, it seemed more like a prison. All outward-facing doors and windows were blocked up; extra walls were built to close off access to the water; and a pair of sturdy iron gates were placed at either end of the bridge leading to Cannaregio. These were closed at sunset and opened in the morning at the ringing of the marangona bell. And just to be sure that no one could sneak out when they weren’t supposed to, four guards – paid for by the Jews themselves – patrolled the canals around the Ghetto ‘day and night’.

It was not the first time that Jews had ever been confined to a separate quarter, of course. By the early 16th century, Jews in France and in German lands had already been living in designated neighbourhoods, physically distinct from the surrounding areas, for close on 300 years. Nor was it even the first time Venice itself had toyed with the idea of Jewish confinement. Back in the 13th century, it had already obliged Jews in its Cretan colony’s capital Candia (now Heraklion) to live in a separate area.

What made the Ghetto unusual was its name. Etymologically speaking, of course, the word geto had nothing to do with Jews. Derived from the verb gettare, meaning ‘to throw’ or ‘cast’, it was just the local name for a foundry (geto) – and, by extension, for the dump next door. But even after the Venetian government moved the foundry elsewhere, people kept on calling the area by its old name. And when the Jews moved in, the island soon lent its name to the institution of segregation, too – a bit like how, today, we can use ‘the White House’ to refer both to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue and to the administration that’s based there.

This was no small matter. Before then, Jewish quarters had been known by all sorts of different names (Judenstraße, Judengasse, Juiverie, etc). But none of them had ever broken through into common parlance as a way of describing segregation per se. They were either too closely associated with a specific geographical feature – a street or a square – or so imprecise that they could refer to just about anything. ‘Ghetto’ offered something different. Precisely because the word was being used metonymically, rather than just geographically, the word ‘ghetto’ could be used to describe any Jewish segregation anywhere. And soon enough, that’s exactly what happened. In around 1562, people started calling the Jewish quarter in Rome a ‘ghetto’; and less than 10 years later, another ‘ghetto’ was established in Florence. And so it went on – right through the 17th century, down to the eve of the French Revolution.

That was just the beginning. After Jewish segregation was abolished in Italy, in the wake of the Napoleonic invasions, the word ‘ghetto’ came to be applied even more widely. Now that its link with a specific type of Jewish segregation was broken, it could denote many more varieties of confinement, marginalisation and exclusion. Brought to the United States in the late 19th century, it was used to describe the poverty and precarity of any migrant group. And after the Nazi invasion of Poland in September 1939, it was applied with terrifying potency to sites of captivity and genocide. Even today, its meanings continue to multiply. Open a newspaper or shuffle your playlist, and you’ll find it used to stigmatise an ‘other’ – or, more often, to reclaim a lost power. And though all these ‘ghettos’ are very different, they all trace their origins back to Venice.

When the Venetian Ghetto was established, of course, no one could have foreseen that it would have such a lasting legacy. Its founders never meant to lay down a marker for the future. It wasn’t the result of a long-term plan. In fact, it almost didn’t happen at all. It was a compromise that emerged out of a period of confusion, experimentation and failure – an attempt to balance the apparently irreconcilable demands of religious prejudice and economic need. It was a paradox, born of war and migration, fear and uncertainty. And, to understand how it came into being, we have to go right back to the arrival of the very first Jews in the Venetian lagoon.

By the time the Ghetto was founded, Jews were already a familiar presence in the Venetian lagoon. As early as the 10th century, Jewish merchants from the eastern Mediterranean are known to have travelled on board Venetian ships; and at least a few spent some time in the city itself. They were, however, a transitory presence, staying only for as long as it took to unload a cargo or conclude their business, and then moving on to harbours new.

Towards the middle of the 14th century, however, a new wave of Jewish migrants began arriving from Germany. These ebrei Tedeschi (German Jews) were not visitors, pausing in the middle of a journey, but refugees. Having been forced to flee their native land by the waves of persecution unleashed by the Black Death, they came to Venice in search of safety – and in the hope of sharing in its commercial might. They first settled in Mestre, just across the lagoon from the city. And they quickly flourished. Some became labourers, others merchants, tailors or jewel-cutters. There were even a few doctors. But it was as money-lenders – or, more properly, pawnbrokers – that they found their niche.

Their success was hardly accidental. Since the mid-12th century, Christians had been forbidden to lend each other money at interest (a practice known as usury). To be sure, some enterprising souls had found a way round this – at least insofar as larger sums were concerned. Were a banker to lend a merchant 2,000 ducats to speculate on wood, for example, he could always dress up the loan as a ‘partnership’, and pretend that the interest was just his share of the profits. But smaller loans were another matter. If a sailor needed to borrow 2 ducats to buy food for his family, and agreed to pay it back, with a bit extra, a month later – well, that was usury, pure and simple. And that’s where the Jews of Mestre came in. As the Fourth Lateran Council had noted, usury was forbidden only between people of the same faith. Provided interest rates were not ‘excessive’, however, there was no reason why Jews couldn’t lend money to Christians. So, by lending small sums – the equivalent of today’s payday loans – the ebrei Tedeschi were able to fill a major gap. And the Venetian government was only too glad for them to do so. More likely than not, in 1366, several German Jews signed a contract (condotta) with the chief magistrate of Mestre, granting them protected status, in exchange for keeping their interest rates down.

No sooner had Venice recovered its prosperity than the ‘need’ for toleration of Jewish migrants began to wane

However, what the ebrei Tedeschi really wanted was to live in Venice itself. But the Venetians were having none of it. Although they were happy enough to borrow money from Jewish bankers when it suited them, they still regarded the same bankers with undisguised hostility. In the Venetians’ eyes, Jews posed a clear and present danger to the Christian faith. If they were allowed to take up residence in the city, the thinking went, they could easily ‘infect’ unsuspecting believers – and thereby undermine the health of Christian society as a whole. There was no question of them being allowed in.

It didn’t take long for Venice to change its mind, though. After a devastating war with Genoa, the Venetian economy was in ruins. Trade had dropped, food prices had soared, and poverty was rising fast. With more people borrowing than ever before, interest rates skyrocketed. If Venice was to stand any chance of getting back on its feet, it needed cheap credit – and fast. Therefore, it put pragmatism ahead of prejudice. In February 1382, the Venetian government offered any banker who would agree to lower their interest rates the chance to live in the city for a period of five years. Theoretically, anyone could apply; but, with only one exception, all those who signed up were Jewish.

It worked like a dream. Little by little, the Venetian economy began to recover. The government was so happy, in fact, that just three years later it voted to offer the ebrei Tedeschi a new condotta, allowing them to go on living in Venice for another decade, after the last arrangement expired. And that wasn’t all. The Venetians were so keen to attract more Jewish bankers to the city that the government even decided to set aside a quarter especially for Jews. In the event, nothing came of this – but the intention was clearly to give Jews a more settled status, and to make Venice a more attractive home for Jewish migrants. A bright future seemed to lie ahead.

But no sooner had Venice recovered its prosperity than the ‘need’ for such toleration began to wane and prejudice once again reared its ugly head. Disagreements sprang up. Threats were made. And, after briefly reviving the plan to create a separate Jewish quarter – albeit to segregate, rather than to welcome the community – the Venetian government decreed that, when the condotta expired in 1397, the Jews would have to leave.

With no other choice, the ebrei Tedeschi dolefully made their way back to Mestre. Although they were not forbidden to visit Venice, they would be allowed to stay only for 15 days at a time and were required to wear a yellow circle on their outer clothing at all times, so that they could be clearly identified – an obligation that had already been foisted on their coreligionists in Sicily, and which would subsequently be imposed in many other Italian cities.

However, the Venetian government quickly realised that it had made a mistake. Although it had seemed easy enough to get rid of the Jews, it proved almost impossible to do without them. Even at a time of economic recovery, ordinary people still needed Jewish loans – and, despite everything, the Jewish moneylenders still wanted their business. It did not take the ebrei Tedeschi long to find a way round the ban. After their 15 days in Venice were up, they simply took a boat to Mestre, stopped for as short a time as was needed to reset the clock, and then went straight back to the city. In this way, they were able to maintain an almost permanent presence in Venice – without ever ‘officially’ residing there.

Naturally, the Venetian authorities tried to clamp down on such infractions. In 1402, they decreed that, after the 15 days were up, Jews could not return to the city for another four months. But there were so many exceptions that it was virtually impossible to enforce. Therefore, even though the Venetian government had no intention of revoking the Jews’ expulsion, it had to reconcile itself to the fact that a Jewish presence of sorts was inevitable – even desirable. As such, its approach shifted from expulsion to containment. Efforts were made to enforce the wearing of the yellow circle, to prohibit acts of worship, and to prevent ‘sexual pollution’. By the 1420s, however, there were just as many Jews in Venice as ever.

Such pragmatic ambiguity might easily have continued indefinitely, had a new wave of antisemitic hostility not swept Europe in the mid-15th century. In response to a complaint from King John II of Castile about the ‘scandalous’ offences Jews were supposedly committing against Christians in his kingdom, Pope Eugenius IV promulgated a bull – Dudum ad nostram audientiam (1442) – that attempted to separate the two religions as completely as possible. All the privileges Jews had previously enjoyed were annulled; harsh new legal restrictions were imposed; and the opportunities for social interaction were cut down to an absolute minimum. Officially, this was intended to apply only to Castile; but in Italy, the mendicant orders were not slow to pick up on its implications. Wandering from town to town, itinerant friars like Domenico da Leonessa preached against Jewish usury and urged municipal authorities to expel Jewish populations once and for all.

This was easier said than done. As Venice had already recognised, most towns depended so much on Jewish credit that it was difficult to imagine doing without them. The friars therefore proposed a solution. With the papacy’s approval, they proposed that towns should set up monti di pietà (‘banks of compassion’). Funded by voluntary donations, these would offer small loans to the working poor on a charitable basis – that is to say, either without asking for any interest at all, or charging rates no higher than they needed to cover their running costs. In principle, this would then relieve Italian towns of the need for Jewish moneylenders, while still respecting the prohibition on Christians lending money.

Several towns had already banned Jews from lending money, or expelled them outright

The first reliably attested monte di pietà was established in Perugia in April 1462. Over the subsequent decades, dozens more followed across Italy and, in most cases, they worked pretty much exactly as the friars had hoped. Once a ‘bank of compassion’ was operating, Italian towns generally didn’t waste much time before ordering the local Jews to leave.

In the Republic of Venice, the friars’ message struck a chord. Since the 1420s, many of Venice’s nearby subject towns on the Italian mainland had grown increasingly hostile to their Jewish residents. Shortly after the promulgation of Dudum ad nostram audientiam, several of them had already banned Jews from lending money, or expelled them outright. And that was just the beginning. When, in 1475, the Jews in Trent (now Trentino) were arrested on suspicion of having ritually murdered a toddler named Simon, a new wave of antisemitic fury was unleashed. Encouraged by preachers like Bernardino da Feltre and Marco da Montegallo, this led to the establishment of monti di pietà in Vicenza, Brescia and Verona just a few years later.

Venice itself seemed close to following suit. Although the Jews’ contribution to the city’s financial stability ultimately prevented the government from taking any precipitous steps just yet, a growing number of patricians were anxious to see them gone. To many of them, it must have seemed like a matter of when, not if.

Their confidence was misplaced, however. When King Charles VIII of France set out to conquer Naples in 1494, Italy was plunged into a series of devastating wars that would rage, on and off, for much of the following 65 years. Venice could not help being drawn into the fray. Yet if it hoped to profit from the fighting, it was cruelly mistaken. It was woefully unprepared. And as its military position worsened, it found that it had no choice but to call on the Jews for help. Heavy taxes and loans were asked of Jewish communities throughout the terraferma (mainland); and, with food prices rising by the day, Venice did whatever it could to keep Jewish credit flowing. On 14 January 1503, the government offered the Jewish bankers of Mestre a new condotta on unusually generous terms. Provided they continued to lend money at reasonable rates of interest, they would be allowed to come and go as they wanted, to rent houses in Venice, and to observe their rites. Most importantly, they were also given an assurance that, if the war on terraferma threatened their safety at any point, they would be allowed to take refuge in Venice itself, and to remain there as long as necessary.

This last clause was probably just meant to be a sweetener. Although Venice was struggling on the battlefield, things were not so bad that anyone seriously expected the bankers of Mestre to flee. But, before long, all that would change. Following a catastrophic defeat at the Battle of Agnadello on 14 May 1509, Venice’s control over the terraferma suddenly collapsed. As French troops advanced on the lagoon, refugees began to stream into the city – including hundreds of Jews from Mestre and other subject cities. The bankers who had signed the 1503 condotta came with the government’s blessing, but a great many more did not.

Terrified that this sudden influx of people would cause a shortage of food, the Venetian government tried desperately to expel anyone who did not have permission to stay. But the frightened refugees refused to budge – and no amount of cajoling could persuade them to do otherwise. Quite suddenly, Venice found itself confronted with precisely the Jewish presence it had tried for so long to avoid.

Even the Jews’ most ardent detractors had to admit that having Jewish bankers in the city at a time of crisis was something of a boon

A paradoxical situation now began to unfold. As the months passed, pressure on the government to expel the Jews – or even worse – only grew. Despite a few fleeting moments of hope, Venice’s position remained critical; and more than once, the city itself was threatened with a direct assault. In the eyes of its inhabitants, every setback began to assume a religious significance. Encouraged by preachers, they came to believe that their misfortunes were a form of divine punishment and that the Jews were ultimately to blame. At Eastertide – when Jews were traditionally held responsible for Christ’s crucifixion – the calls for retribution became intense. On 2 April 1511, for example, Fra Rufin Lovato suggested that the best course of action would be ‘to deprive [Jews] of everything they owned and put them to the sack’.

At the same time, it was increasingly clear to the government that it would not just be difficult to remove the Jews – but positively dangerous to do so. Even the Jews’ most ardent detractors had to admit that having Jewish bankers in the city at a time of crisis was something of a boon. The diarist Marin Sanudo the Younger is a case in point. Although he complained bitterly about the ‘great number’ of Jews he saw in the street, he acknowledged that it was impossible to say anything because ‘they are needed’. And the more the war dragged on, the more essential they became.

The question facing Venice therefore shifted. Instead of focusing on how the Jews might be expelled, the government now began to ask itself how best it could take advantage of the Jews’ presence, while minimising the ‘risk’.

It was not long before a new ‘solution’ presented itself. On 23 April 1515 – 18 months after the Venetian defeat at the Battle of Schio – Giorgio Emo, an important member of the Collegio – the nearest thing Venice had to a cabinet – proposed that the Jews should be confined to the island of Giudecca. It seemed to be a reasonable compromise. There, Emo argued, the Jews would be kept far enough away from the Christian population to prevent religious ‘infection’ from spreading, yet close enough that they could keep the wheels of finance turning. Naturally, the Jews were appalled. They protested that, if the Jewish community was forced to move to Giudecca, it would be in danger of being attacked by the mercenaries billeted there. They therefore suggested the island of Murano instead. But when this, too, turned out to be unworkable, Emo’s proposal was quietly shelved. The principle of segregation was not in any doubt, though. It was just that, for the moment, the government didn’t have the time – or the inclination – to find a more suitable location.

It didn’t take much for that to change. The following year, the Emperor Maximilian invaded the Duchy of Milan, threatening the security of Venice’s remaining possessions on terraferma. In Venice itself, public anxiety rose. That Easter, Fra Lovato once again railed against the Jews. His sermons were apparently no more violent than before. But it was enough to revive the idea of segregation – and stirred the government to action. On 26 March 1516, the Venetian patrician Zaccaria Dolfin presented a proposal to the Collegio similar in outline to that put forward by Emo the previous year. Dolfin stressed that the Jewish presence was the source of Venice’s ills. Given that the Jews could neither be expelled nor confined too far from the city’s markets, he therefore proposed that they should be sent to live on the island of the geto novo in Cannaregio. Despite strong opposition from the Jewish community, the Collegio approved the proposal and, three days later, the Senate confirmed its decision. On 1 April, city criers read the decree in public, and by 25 July, all Venice’s Jews, without exception, were in the geto novo. The Ghetto had been born.

The Ghetto was never meant to be anything more than a temporary measure – a quick fix for a passing ‘problem’. But over the decades that followed, the persistence of war and an abiding reluctance to establish a monte di pietà in Venice prevented the government from ridding itself of the city’s Jewish quarter. In fact, as time wore on, the steady decline of Venice’s fortunes not only guaranteed the Ghetto’s endurance – it also paved the way for its expansion. Later, two further ghettos would be created – the Ghetto Vecchio (1541) and the Ghetto Nuovissimo (1633) – each intended to accommodate different groups of Jewish migrants from the Iberian peninsula (those who came via the Ottoman Empire being known euphemistically as ‘Levantines’, and those who subsequently arrived by a more direct route as ‘Ponentines’), whose involvement in international trade increasingly sustained Venice’s faltering commercial standing. And though the Ghetto itself would endure its own decline, it would not be abolished until after the arrival of Napoleon in 1797.

The Ghetto was, from its inception, a site of exclusion. As the centuries wore on, efforts were repeatedly made to reinforce the barriers – both real and metaphorical – that separated its inhabitants from the Christian world beyond. Yet at no point was it ever hermetically sealed. Its very existence was founded on the necessity of exchange, interaction, even co-existence. The credit market, and later international trade, required there to be a constant to-ing and fro-ing between Jews and Christians. Exactly the same was true of cultural life. In a city as intellectually vibrant as Venice, where humanists were as fascinated by anything Hebrew as they were by Latin and Greek, the exchange of ideas was inevitable. And this is to say nothing of the fact that identities in early modern Venice were often so complicated that it was virtually impossible to separate any communities completely.

In some ways, then, the Ghetto is a reminder of the paradox that lies at the heart of all forms of social exclusion, even today. It speaks to the fact that any attempt to marginalise a community ultimately arises out of ties that bind – and speaks more eloquently to the failures of those doing the marginalisation than it does to any perceived ‘differences’.

Yet perhaps the Ghetto’s most powerful lesson for our own times lies in its contingency. The path to its foundation was not travelled in giant leaps, but in hesitant steps. It was made up of small, incremental decisions, each of which was contested – and all of which seemed conditional, at best, in the moment. At any stage, it could have been stopped. Venice could have reversed its steps or chosen a different road. And this is where its real message lies. Today, antisemitism is once again on the rise, influenced by wars beyond our reach, and events beyond our control. It is built on paradoxes and contradictions, prejudices and failures. And it advances by small steps – steps that we tell ourselves are isolated or unrepresentative in themselves. A piece of graffiti, a shouted slogan, a casual assault in the street. But Venice shows where those steps lead – and reminds us that every one can, and must, be fought.

item.title: I won’t remain alone
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
In the wake of tragedy, an elderly couple must make a choice: should they let their son go to save the lives of others?

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
The Iranian filmmaker Yaser Talebi brings human stories to the screen with care and empathy, lending a poetic framing to the lives of ordinary people. This sensibility shapes his documentary I Won’t Remain Alone. Set in northern Iran, the film tells the story of an elderly couple in a small village whose son has been pronounced brain dead after a tragic accident. When doctors approach them about authorising his organs to be donated, they’re left with an agonising decision: to let their son go so that someone else’s life might continue. Talebi stays close to the couple as they weigh the choice, capturing the grief that envelops their lives and the powerful consequences of their ultimate decision.

For more from Talebi, watch Sarnevesht (Daughter), which follows an 18-year-old girl in rural Iran as she struggles to balance education and family.

item.title: How to assemble science
item.dc:creator: Helen Pearson
item.description:
Humanity produces a staggering amount of new knowledge every day. The question is how to make sense of it all

- by Helen Pearson

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

26 minute listen

When reading the news, you may occasionally be bemused by the flip-flopping science and health stories: one week you’re told coffee is good for you, the next week that it’s bad. Red wine extends your life, then it doesn’t. Over time, new scientific studies seemingly contradict one another, leaving us unsure what evidence to believe.

As a science journalist, I’ve learnt that often the actual problem is that each study is reported in isolation, rather than weighed against everything else we know. And sometimes, the risks of harm are high. For example, in September 2025, I reported on the US Food and Drug Administration’s announcement that it would add a warning label to the painkiller acetaminophen (paracetamol), claiming that taking the drug during pregnancy increased a child’s risk of autism. It made global headlines. Yet looking closer at the science, it was clear that the FDA and its parent health department had cherrypicked a few studies, and downplayed other more robust findings. This was confirmed a couple of months later when researchers published a major review that better represented the full body of knowledge. ‘Existing evidence does not clearly link maternal paracetamol use during pregnancy with autism or ADHD in offspring,’ it concluded. By then, of course, countless women had been needlessly scared about a painkiller that is widely considered one of the safest to take during pregnancy.

In 2025, academics worldwide published about 7 million scholarly articles ­– that’s more than 19,000 each day. On the surface, that might seem like a number to celebrate, but it also poses a problem. As the volume of research balloons, it can be hard to discern what these millions of papers actually tell us. Within the firehose, there are rigorous methodologies and important findings, but also baffling contradictions, unconfirmed results and sloppy science. And some diverse forms of knowledge, such as lived experience and Indigenous insights, are rarely captured in scholarly articles and databases at all.

The causes are systemic. Scientists publish and promote one paper after another because that’s how they advance in their careers. Journalists breathlessly chase the latest, flashiest studies so their headlines get clicks online. Meanwhile, hardly any of us spend time trying to make sense of what the world already knows by carefully synthesising and taking stock of existing knowledge. Iain Chalmers, a doctor who co-founded the Cochrane Collaboration, an evidence-synthesis group based in London, once called this the ‘scandalous failure of science to cumulate evidence scientifically’.

This failure was a key motivation to write my book Beyond Belief: How Evidence Shows What Really Works (2026). Researching it, I discovered better ways to make sense of the world – but these methods are not as widely known as they should be. If they were, we might pause before believing news stories based on single studies, and instead recognise the real work: finding, sorting and synthesising evidence. This unglamorous labour already shapes our lives far more than any individual study or news headline will. We might also realise that, for many of the wicked problems we face, humans already possess much of the knowledge needed to solve them. All it needs is the ability to assemble it – and then act.

One of the biggest events in the history of evidence synthesis occurred in a hotel in San Francisco in 1976. There, at the annual meeting of the American Educational Research Association, the statistician Gene Glass revealed an ingenious technique that showed how to integrate findings from a large volume of individual studies. This technique would become so important to science that it has its own biography.

Glass’s work had emerged from his own struggles with mental health. A decade earlier, when he had finished his PhD in psychometrics and statistics, he was suffering from anxiety and neurosis. He began weekly psychotherapy sessions – which helped him hugely – and stayed in therapy for eight years. But his positive experience ran counter to the weight of academic opinion, which maintained that psychotherapy had little benefit. This stemmed in large part from the work of the psychologist Hans Eysenck, whose influential reviews of psychotherapy research concluded that it was worthless – or had a placebo effect at best.

Glass was irritated. Not only did this suggest that he’d flushed away money on ineffective therapy, but he felt Eysenck’s reviewing methods were flawed.

Eysenck – like other researchers at the time – tended to do what’s called ‘vote-counting’: counting up the number of studies showing a treatment has benefits, and the number that did not find it helped. The one with the most ‘votes’ wins. Intuitive though vote-counting is, it’s also misleading as a way of synthesising studies, partly because it ignores the size of the effects. One study may find that 55 people out of 100 improved after a particular treatment, and another that 85 out of 100 did. Even though the second study showed the treatment had a much stronger effect, both studies contribute one vote. Glass could see this was problematic ­– and was also astonished that Eysenck arbitrarily excluded hundreds of valid studies just because they were in theses or dissertations rather than published in academic journals.

The audience was thunderstruck. Here was a way to extract meaning from an apparent mess of different results

Glass set out to do a better job. He and his wife, a psychologist named Mary Lee Smith, systematically hunted down every scrap of research they could find that compared the effect of psychotherapy with a control group or another therapy – ending up with more than 370 studies.

Then Glass and Smith worked out a way to extract and combine the measurements of psychotherapy’s effect in each study. Even though one study measured the effects of the therapy on anxiety and another its impact on blood pressure, they devised a way to convert these results into one standard measure known as ‘effect size’ and then average them across all the studies. (This is somewhat like converting various currencies into dollars, so they can all be combined.) Glass called this new statistical method a meta-analysis – an analysis of analyses, just as metadata is data about data.

After toiling on this work for two years, Glass and Smith concluded that psychotherapy had a beneficial effect, and Glass presented the method at the San Francisco hotel where the education meeting was taking place. Debate continues to this day about whether psychotherapy works, when and for whom. (Eysenck called the work ‘an exercise in mega-silliness’.) But of the meta-analysis, the audience was thunderstruck. Here was a way to extract meaning from an apparent mess of different results.

The meta-analysis was not the only synthesis tool to emerge around this time. The work of Glass, Smith and other researchers also led to the systematic review, a rigorously structured method for gathering and evaluating evidence. In a systematic review, researchers scour databases worldwide of published and unpublished work for all studies that address a certain question. Then they whittle down a longlist of thousands of studies to the most relevant few, assess their reliability, extract the data, and combine the results. Many systematic reviews include a meta-analysis to pool results from the included studies and estimate the overall effect of a treatment or other intervention.

These tools to make sense of a body of evidence are one of the most important developments in science over the past few decades. They have the power to identify important conclusions that would never be possible from assessing each underlying study on its own. It’s the scientific equivalent of seeing the forest, not just the trees.

Without fanfare, these approaches have changed modern life – and particularly so when it comes to health decisions. In medicine, this happened partly thanks to a morning stroll by Iain Chalmers, an early champion of evidence synthesis, along the Wolvercote Mill Stream in Oxford, UK, in May 1991.

Chalmers had just finished a pioneering, decade-long project to synthesise all the evidence from clinical trials on treatments in pregnancy and childbirth. This work, which involved doing hundreds of systematic reviews, had shown that many standard medical practices – such as shaving women’s pubic hair during labour, and surgical episiotomies – were based on little evidence and some were harmful. The work from Chalmers and his colleagues helped change some of these practices.

Now Chalmers was thinking about expanding this work. Wouldn’t it be useful, he thought, to synthesise clinical trials in every area of medicine and healthcare? Then doctors and patients would know, based on evidence, effective ways of treating diabetes, cancer, heart disease and many other conditions. Surprisingly, many medical decisions at that time were based on conventional wisdom or the unsubstantiated opinions of senior doctors rather than on evidence from research.

Some years earlier, in 1979, a doctor called Archie Cochrane working in Cardiff, Wales, had challenged the medical community to do just this. ‘It is surely a great criticism of our profession that we have not organised a critical summary, by speciality or subspecialty, adapted periodically, of all relevant randomised controlled trials,’ Cochrane wrote. Chalmers was greatly influenced by Cochrane, and he was now ready to take on the task. He and his team started searching for clinical trials in online academic databases and scouring journals by hand in the library. The task was so big that they recruited volunteers to join the hunt, including elderly people’s groups and even the unlikely source of the Headington Bowls Club in Oxford. Soon, they had tens of thousands of trials.

Most people who have seen a Western doctor have unknowingly benefited from systematic reviews

But Chalmers knew that synthesising all the evidence on effective treatments in medicine was such a gargantuan task that it would take more people power than this. So, in 1993, he and a group of like-minded folk started the Cochrane Collaboration (now known as just Cochrane), dedicated to producing high-quality systematic reviews of evidence on the effectiveness of health treatments.

Within 10 years of starting, the Cochrane Collaboration had published around 2,000 systematic reviews and was helping to popularise this type of study. By 2010, researchers inside and outside the collaboration were publishing 11 systematic reviews on healthcare every day.

Today, the ‘Cochrane review’ is known for being one of the most rigorous and reliable syntheses of science, and systematic reviews are used to develop the clinical guidelines that doctors use to guide decisions. Most people who have seen a Western doctor have unknowingly benefited from systematic reviews. They have become an invisible bedrock of evidence on which medicine is based.

To understand what the world would look like without them, consider this notorious piece of medical advice that went unchallenged in the mid-20th century. In 1957, the paediatrician Benjamin Spock made a small change to the second edition of his parenting bestseller The Common Sense Book of Baby and Childcare (1946), reissued several more times over the years. He said that parents should put babies to sleep on their fronts rather than on their backs. By the 1980s and ’90s, studies were clearly showing that this was one of the most lethal pieces of unsubstantiated advice in the history of child health, as it contributed to a steep rise in sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

What makes this story even more tragic is that the link between sleeping position and SIDS might have been detected earlier – if researchers had synthesised the evidence from studies rather than looking at them one at a time. When researchers did this with a systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2005, they discovered that the link between front-sleeping and SIDS was clear in 1970, some 20 years before most parents were warned about the risks. They calculated that at least 50,000 infant deaths in Europe, Australasia and the United States might have been prevented if evidence had been synthesised and acted on earlier.

Medicine is not the only field to have built up a repository of evidence syntheses. Other disciplines – ranging from conservation to education – have mimicked the medical model.

The nonprofit International Initiative for Impact Evaluation holds more than 1,700 systematic reviews on what works in international development, such as improving sanitation and tackling malnourishment. CEEDER, a major environmental database, hosts more than 2,100 evidence reviews on what works to save species and protect the planet.

The Education Endowment Foundation, a nonprofit organisation in London dedicated to boosting learning outcomes for disadvantaged children, has constructed a widely admired ‘teaching and learning toolkit’ using systematic reviews of studies that have tested education approaches. Nearly 70 per cent of school leaders in England now use it to make spending decisions, and it has been adapted for use in more than 30 countries and translated into nine languages.

The IPCC’s syntheses have helped to inspire global action by showing that humans are causing climate change

One of the most effective strategies, it shows, is teaching students metacognition – the ability to learn how to learn. (For instance, a child who learns that writing out the steps helped her solve a maths problem is practising metacognition.) Introducing metacognition provides children with an impressive eight months of additional learning progress, on average, over a year, according to the evidence review. Repeating a school year, by contrast, sets back students’ learning by about two months.

More recently, climate scientists have been taking a leaf out of medicine’s book. They are used to synthesising evidence: the six massive scientific assessments that the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has published since 1988 are probably the biggest and most influential evidence syntheses ever done – helping inspire global action by showing that humans are causing climate change. But the IPCC reports have so far said less about solutions, such as which climate policies could help the most.

A group called What Works Climate Solutions, which started in 2024, is now striving to build a Cochrane-like bank of evidence syntheses that show the most effective ways to cut emissions or adapt to global warming. This evidence bank will feed into the next scientific assessment of the IPCC, due to be published by late 2029, and should help governments choose which policies to adopt.

The soaring popularity of systematic reviews is visible in academic databases. The number published in medicine alone rose from around 1,400 in the year 2000 to more than 29,000 in 2019 – about 80 per day. A set of guidelines for performing them accurately, called PRISMA, has become one of the most cited papers of the 21st century – with as many as 138,000 citations, by one count.

Systematic reviews have their critics. One is that they conventionally emphasise quantitative studies – those with numerical data – and ignore qualitative research, such as that based on interviews and observations. There is a lively debate going on among evidence-synthesis experts about how best to integrate different streams of information.

In some fields, such as conservation, scientists have been reproached for privileging Western science over other forms of knowledge, such as the lived experience of local communities and Indigenous groups. Some Indigenous peoples in Canada, for example, have extensive knowledge of the behaviours of the migratory fish that they hunt. These types of evidence don’t fit in conventional reviews that just crunch numbers.

But there are ways to combine them. In 2021, Parks Canada and a group called Foundations of Success undertook an extraordinary analysis of evidence to decide whether to pursue an expensive and risky captive breeding programme for endangered caribou in Jasper National Park. As well as collecting a range of evidence from research, they asked people from Indigenous groups, zoos, and reindeer experts from Finland, to review the evidence and reach agreement about whether to proceed. (They did – and some adorable caribou calves were born in 2025.)

Over the past few decades, researchers have developed a suite of methods for combining evidence of different types. Some pool only qualitative studies, while other ‘mixed-methods’ syntheses combine qualitative and quantitative work. Some researchers who supply evidence to busy government policymakers favour the rapid review, which involves getting together the best evidence synthesis you can, to answer their question in the time available – which could be the next day. They prefer a good synthesis delivered on time rather than a perfect one that arrives too late.

Studies that claim to provide an overview of evidence convey authority, so scientists have a responsibility to get them right

Elsewhere, scientists have been working on another important innovation called living reviews. These are updated frequently and continuously as research is published rather than, as often happens, a static systematic review that quickly becomes out of date. Living reviews can be labour intensive and so are most worthwhile for important questions on which new studies are being published quickly. During the COVID-19 pandemic, a handful of groups soon rallied and developed living reviews to synthesise rapidly emerging studies on COVID therapies and vaccines.

The methods used for synthesising science have become so complex over the past 20 years that evidence synthesis has become a profession in its own right. There are entire journals dedicated to the craft, as well as academic centres, professorships and prizes. As a science journalist, I’ve interviewed evidence geeks who can talk for hours about the finer details of systematic reviews.

And sometimes tensions bubble up about the best way to synthesise a body of research. A purist argues that a gold-standard systematic review is the most rigorous way of doing it and that other methods risk missing studies or including poor-quality work and thus reaching the wrong conclusion. A pragmatist argues that a systematic review takes too long, and that often a quick-and-dirty aluminium-standard synthesis will do.

But, really, this is a storm in a teacup. Different methods for evidence synthesis suit different situations. What’s important is to be transparent about the methods used and any weaknesses they have. Studies that claim to provide a rigorous overview of evidence convey authority, so scientists have a heavy responsibility to get them right.

In a world where a news story or a social media post can spread in hours, one of the biggest problems in systematic reviewing is the time it takes. An analysis of more than 500 Cochrane reviews found that a review typically took nearly three years ­– and one took a glacial eight. That’s because doing a systematic review involves working through around 25 steps – carefully finding, filtering, and combining studies – of which many are even done in duplicate to avoid errors. This exacting process explains why many researchers view with horror the prospect of doing a systematic review.

Researchers have long used computers to help, but the rapid advances in generative AI are fuelling new excitement about accelerating and automating the task. Could AI help make sense of the overwhelmingly large scientific literature?

It has changed the way I think about research as a science journalist and in everyday life

Start-ups are racing to develop AI-powered systems that can find, sort and summarise research publications, but most have not yet been well tested and shown reliably to produce high-quality systematic reviews. Even so, it seems inevitable that they will improve and that before too long most of the grunt work involved in compiling evidence will routinely be done by machines, freeing up humans to check and interpret the results. That could mean that anyone would be able to assemble a reliable evidence synthesis tailored to their question, virtually at the push of a button – an appealing goal.

But it’s still some way off – and concerns about AI and evidence synthesis also abound. One is that AI is leading to a flood of inaccurate scientific reviews because researchers are using these tools to race through poor-quality efforts. Another is that people will bypass rigorous evidence syntheses entirely: because why bother, when you can just ask ChatGPT what the evidence says? (This is currently dangerous as AI tools can hallucinate and give an inaccurate picture, and most do not have access to the full corpus of the world’s research.)

One lesson from all this is to be aware that single studies can be outliers – something I’ve learned myself over the past few years. I’ve spoken with hundreds of researchers worldwide about the importance of synthesising evidence, and it has changed the way I think about research as a science journalist and in everyday life. Now, when I speak to scientists about their latest study, I try to ask how it fits with the wider body of research. When seeking evidence on a personal issue, such as a medical diagnosis, I tend to search for systematic reviews and other syntheses (while being aware that not all reviews are good quality).

We should resist the allure and glamour of new studies. It’s true that new research is important, because it leads to innovation and fresh ways to protect the planet and human lives. But if we truly want to understand the world and make it a better place, we also need to do the less glamorous, unappreciated work of collating existing knowledge – and figuring out what it all means.

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
In the experimental short All-around Junior Male, the Inuk filmmaker Lindsay McIntyre documents a traditional Inuit game known as the one-foot high kick. Competitors attempt to leap from both feet to strike a suspended target, landing on the same foot used to kick, with the target rising after each successful round. The game was once used by hunters to indicate a successful hunt and demands extraordinary strength, balance and control. In her portrait, McIntyre captures the Nunamiut athlete Sean Uquqtuq in action with monochrome, hand-processed film that abstracts the landscape around him, focusing on his face and the movement of his body. Combined with an ambient score, these elements lend the piece an immersive, dreamlike quality.
