item.title: Reasoning together
item.dc:creator: Emilie Prattico
item.description:
Jürgen Habermas, the great defender of deliberative democracy, lived up to its demands: he never feared changing his mind

- by Emilie Prattico

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

22 minute listen

Jürgen Habermas died on 14 March 2026, in the German town of Starnberg, aged 96. Every fall, from the mid-1990s into the late-2000s, he would come to Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois to teach and give talks, a visit that a dedicated group of students looked forward to every fall term. The year that has stayed with me is 2004, when he taught what he’d spelled out in Between Facts and Norms (1992), his opus applying his theory to democratic politics. Law, philosophy, history, political science: students spanned many disciplines to come watch the famous German scholar every week, dressed in Wrangler jeans and a tweed jacket, expose his theory of deliberative politics in his unmistakable nasal voice, thick German accent, and impeccable English. Max Weber and the Frankfurt School, which were intimate to him, since he’d been Theodor Adorno’s research assistant in the 1950s, came to life in his speech and then in schemas and figures in chalk as he theorised about them.

I understood almost none of it at first: words I’d read were coming to life in the room, spoken by their author, and still not resolving into sense. After several lectures, the shape came into focus: this wasn’t just Between Facts and Norms being rebuilt in public, but decades of work arriving at a single place. Since The Theory of Communicative Action (1981), Habermas had been arguing that reason survives in modern life only as something people do together, that is, by giving each other reasons and staying open to being moved by them, rather than by force, money or tradition. Between Facts and Norms was that idea turned toward law and democracy directly: a state counts as legitimate only when its laws could in principle be justified to everyone bound by them, through exactly that kind of open exchange. I’d watched that argument take root in a decades-long intellectual history. Thinking is a practice, it involves owing each other explanations, questions, answers. It is not a fast process, and doing it in public, out loud, in front of a room, is what makes it worthwhile.

I attended all of Habermas’s seminars during my time at Northwestern with great interest and, to be honest, a sense of awe. One day, the topic of the weekly seminar was inclusion, and I had argued, with the timid conviction of a green graduate student, that deliberative publics ought to be designed for inclusion, and that entry into these publics required that members accept the terms of deliberation themselves. ‘Well, we can tell that Ms Prattico really is a Catholic in the strict, universalist sense,’ was not the answer I expected – and what took me by surprise wasn’t that he’d made a joke of my religion, but that he’d seen me as a person with a history and a set of unexamined beliefs, something he’d noticed only by teaching me.

After the seminars, the class would sometimes go out for drinks. It was on one of these occasions that I understood where the joke had come from. I’d asked him what it had been like arriving in the US as a visiting professor for the first time, at the New School for Social Research in the autumn of 1967, which decades earlier had served as a refuge for scholars fleeing the same Germany in which he’d grown up. It was the start of a long habit of crossing the Atlantic: Princeton four years later, for the Gauss Lectures where he first tried out the turn toward language that would eventually become his theory of communicative action; then, decades on, Northwestern, where I got to sit in the room.

Habermas answered my question by going back further than any of that. He’d been raised Lutheran. Visiting the US in the 1960s and ’70s, he’d been introduced to the Quakers, and something in their small meetings had stayed with him, specifically the way they sought unity with everyone present. When he came to describe the conditions under which people could reason together as equals, he said he heard an echo of those meetings: conditions that hold only when everyone who could be affected by a norm isn’t just included but has a voice, can object, and speaks with sincerity. In those conditions, which go far beyond mere inclusion, the only constraint left on discourse is ‘the unforced force of the better argument’, as he put it in Justification and Application (1993). It didn’t feel like something he’d have said at the podium.

The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962), his seminal work originally published in German, made an argument about something concrete: 18th-century coffeehouses, salons and journals, where private citizens began treating the affairs of state as something they had standing to publicly discuss and judge, rather than simply obey. That habit, Habermas argued, was where modern democratic legitimacy first took root. The book also identified tendencies that would weaken it, too. He thought that the public sphere had already started to decay, folded back into spectacle by advertising and mass media, the public reduced from participants to an audience. It took almost 30 years for an English translation to appear. By the time it did, in 1989, Habermas had gotten a great deal of mileage out of the book in its original language; indeed, it had already made him a name outside Germany. When Craig Calhoun finally gathered the English-language response into a single volume, Habermas and the Public Sphere (1992), bringing together historians and theorists who challenged the argument, closing with a long response from Habermas himself, he could have easily spent the occasion defending a book that had already proved itself. Instead, he very openly contended with these critiques.

He came to think he’d been too sceptical about one piece of that story. But the warning itself never went away

Two critics stand out. Nancy Fraser argued that the public sphere was never actually open to everyone since it had excluded women and other groups from the start. She proposed replacing one public with many, arguing with each other, including publics formed by the very groups shut out of the first one. Geoff Eley made a related point from history: working-class and plebeian public spheres had existed alongside the bourgeois one all along, not before or after it. Both were extending an argument that Oskar Negt and Alexander Kluge had made back in 1972, that a whole proletarian public sphere existed, which Habermas’s book never accounted for.

Habermas answered these criticisms directly, in an essay called ‘Further Reflections on the Public Sphere’, printed as the closing chapter of Calhoun’s book. Habermas conceded that the exclusion of women was not incidental but built into how the bourgeois public sphere had worked from the start. Unlike the exclusion of underprivileged men, which was a problem of class, and in principle correctable, the exclusion of women, he now wrote, ‘has been constitutive for the political public sphere not merely in that the latter has been dominated by men as a matter of contingency but also in that its structure and relation to the private sphere has been determined in a gender-specific fashion.’ Habermas conceded that other public spheres had existed alongside the one he had taken as foundational. And he softened the warning, without abandoning it. He came to think he’d been too sceptical about one piece of that story, the early stirrings of consumer society. But the warning itself never went away. Sixty years on, he was still diagnosing a public sphere being distorted by commercial and structural forces, only now the culprit was platforms and algorithms rather than advertising and mass circulation.

He did not give up everything. He still wanted to keep the public sphere as something to measure democracies against, even if the history behind it was messier than he’d first made it look. The criticism and his answer to it sit in the same book, printed one after the other. Habermas’s views were open to being challenged, and open for us all to witness his thought in process.

Early in my dissertation work, I wanted to explore the role of experts in democracies through Habermas’s theory of deliberative politics, though I didn’t yet know how – I was, by any measure, stuck. My advisor, Cristina Lafont, one of his most trusted students, arranged a meeting anyway, at the hotel where he stayed during his visits to Northwestern’s campus in Evanston. He didn’t seem to mind that I arrived without a fully formed argument. Over almost two hours at what was then the Homestead Hotel, he had me lay out the problem as it stood, half-formed, and began working through it himself, out loud, testing it against his own theory as he went. He explained the three types of discourse that characterise deliberation – moral, ethical, and pragmatic – and was clear that when it comes to the moral, there are no experts: only individuals working out, together, what’s right in a given context.

Followed to its conclusion, that seemed to leave no room for expertise anywhere in deliberative politics. But he then turned to pragmatic discourse, where expertise does real work: finding the most empirically sound way to reach a goal already agreed on. Experts have no authority over what’s right, fair or worth valuing – only over facts. This was, in miniature, an argument he’d been making since his early work on science and politics: that treating value-laden political questions as though they were merely technical ones corrodes democracy. Decades later, in Justification and Application, he’d given the same worry he’d laid out in the trichotomy that morning sharper philosophical shape.

In later meetings in his office, more routine than that first one, I pushed the distinction further: what did it mean for climate change – a problem almost always treated, in his terms, as a matter of pragmatic discourse, all graphs and targets and carbon budgets, and almost never as a moral one. Who pays? What do we owe the people who pay? How should the resources that caused the damage be used? He didn’t have a ready answer. He asked question after question, testing the case against his own framework as though it genuinely hadn’t occurred to him before.

Justification answers only to the standards we happen to hold now: those standards can be shown wrong later

I’ll never know for sure if he was being generous or if I had shown him something he had not yet thought of in applying his own distinction. What stayed with me wasn’t the answer but the manner of it: a philosopher in his 70s, decades into a settled framework, still willing to test that framework against a case he hadn’t considered, in real time, out loud, in front of a student.

By 1999, Habermas gave up a position he’d held since 1973, the year he’d argued that truth is simply whatever people would agree on if they argued it out under fair-enough conditions. By the end of the century, he’d decided this was a mistake: it confused truth with justification. A claim can meet every test we have for it, survive every objection anyone raises, be about as justified as a claim can be, and still turn out false. That’s because justification answers only to the standards we happen to hold right now, and those standards can later be shown wrong. Truth doesn’t move when our standards do. Moral claims were different, he still thought: what’s right can only ever be what a fair conversation would settle on. There’s nothing else for rightness to answer to. But facts about the world answer to the world itself, not just to our best current agreement about it.

Several people had been pushing him toward this change. The US philosopher Richard Rorty pushed from the side from which Habermas was now backing away: for Rorty, there was no need for truth to answer to anything beyond what an audience could be talked into agreeing on, and he’d been making that case to Habermas for years. Lafont, my advisor, who’d arranged the hotel meeting, pushed from the other side, drawing on the US philosopher Hilary Putnam, who had spent much of his career arguing against exactly the kind of view that made truth depend entirely on human agreement. Lafont had argued since 1994 that Habermas’s own philosophical tradition, in its turn toward language, had drifted into a position where it couldn’t say the world holds firm no matter how we talk about it. When Habermas changed his mind, he moved toward Lafont’s position, not Rorty’s.

What Habermas never spelled out is what this does to moral and political claims once people stop being able to agree at all. Truth, on his revised view, still has somewhere to go even if everyone stops talking: the world doesn’t care whether anyone’s listening. His philosophy of Rightness never had that option. So, when the people who’d need to agree on something splinter into groups that no longer talk to each other, a factual claim can still be true or false regardless. A moral claim has nothing left holding it up, once nobody’s left in the room to agree on it.

Habermas gave up a position he’d held for almost 30 years because the people around him showed him it didn’t hold. He’d spent decades arguing that claims get redeemed when someone can compel you to answer, and then was compelled himself, and answered, in print, aged 70. Those critiques were not meant to be damning objections: they were precisely what his theory called for and was built on, ultimately.

Habermas returned to the subject in ‘Reflections and Hypotheses on a Further Structural Transformation of the Political Public Sphere’ (2022). His starting point is a particular relationship between beliefs and reality. Constitutional democracy runs on citizens holding certain assumptions about their own disagreements, namely that the disagreements are real, that they’re about something, that better reasons could in principle settle them. The system holds together only as long as those assumptions stay reasonably close to how politics actually works. His argument is that a public sphere, run through social media, threatens that relationship and widens that gap.

For Habermas, there are two forces at play in this widening. Platforms drop the editorial filtering that newspapers and broadcasters used to perform, and they turn every user into someone who publishes. For Habermas the deeper problem isn’t the resulting noise; it’s that heavy platform use produces something smaller than a public: semi-public spheres, self-enclosed, silos whose members can no longer perceive the wider public sphere as inclusive at all – claims to universality beyond their own horizon become, in his words, ‘suspect of hypocrisy’. That perception is itself the damage, on his account, as much as anything actually happening out in the general public sphere. He ends by insisting that ‘maintaining a media structure that ensures the inclusive character of the public sphere and the deliberative character of the formation of public opinion and political will is not a matter of political preference but a constitutional imperative.’

A factual claim still has to get the world right, whether or not anyone’s around to check it. Moral claims never did: they answer only to discourse. And discourse is exactly what he’s just described coming apart. He doesn’t draw the conclusion for moral and political claims himself, but it follows from putting his two books next to each other: the very thing a claim about what we owe each other had to answer to is the thing he says is disappearing, in an age dominated by exchanges on social media.

People retreat into whichever group agrees with them and lose their grip on a shared standard of true and false

Around that time, I reached out to my advisor for help asking Habermas for a foreword to a collection I was editing on Habermas and democracy. He was known for guarding his time closely – very few people had his email address, and he accepted only a handful of the hundreds of such requests he received each year. A couple of months later, an email came from an address I didn’t recognise: he had accepted, and written to say so himself. Amid the logistics, he added one condition: ‘You should send me at least a substantive part of the book before I can and would sit down and settle a few ideas.’ At 92, he wanted the material in hand before he’d commit to anything.

What came back was not a review of the interviews that make up the book one by one. He says so himself in the opening lines: it isn’t his task to comment on the conversations directly. Instead, he used the occasion to answer the standing objections to his view of deliberative democracy, and to close with the digital transformation that turned out to run through nearly every interview in the book – a theme he noticed himself, and named as central to the collection. One section was on experts, common sense, and the chain of translation that carries specialised knowledge into public reasoning: the same distinction he’d first sketched over a hotel breakfast, worked out now in far more detail, at the very end of his working life.

At one point, he writes that what’s been lost, in the democracies now regressing, is ‘a conflict of opinions that remains recognisable as a dispute about which position is backed by the better reasons.’ That’s as close as he ever came, in anything he wrote for me directly, to stating my own premise in his own words. He names the same loss again later in the foreword, describing people who retreat into whichever group already agrees with them and lose their grip not just on the public sphere’s inclusiveness but on the idea of a shared standard of true and false. What he doesn’t do here, any more than he did in 1999, is follow that loss when it concerns a moral claim once the discourse behind it comes apart. And that is what I tried to explore in my philosophical work since my dissertation.

He still believed the gap between expert and layperson could always, in principle, be closed by the right chain of translation. It was the one thing he never revised: he revised his theory of the public sphere, his theory of truth, but never the conviction that under the right conditions people can still reach each other. I am not persuaded that these conditions are as anywhere close to being met today – but that’s a disagreement I never got to have with him.

item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
The remarkable engineering and tragic demise of the vessel that would end Britain’s dream to dominate the skies

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: In this short video, Bill Hammack, an engineer and professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, details the extraordinary making and tragic ending of the British airship known as R101. Conceived in 1924 and first flown in 1929, R101 was intended to fly a regular route from England to India. Hammack uses archival images and his own deep research to trace the engineering and history of this remarkable vessel, which the British government planned as the flagship of a fleet that would criss-cross its then-sprawling empire. Those ambitious plans were abandoned after the airship crashed in France in October 1930, killing 48 of the 54 people on board. Hammack offers a riveting peek into a brief moment in aviation history – one ended for good by the crash of the Hindenburg in 1937 – when it appeared as if commercial airships might become a regular sight in skies across the world. The video accompanies Hammack’s book Fatal Flight: The True Story of Britain’s Last Great Airship (2017), which is available as a free audiobook at his website.

item.title: Where a land ethic blooms
item.dc:creator: Craig Maier
item.description:
Caring for this planet entails decisions that are intimate, about our farms, our homes, our human and our wild neighbours

- by Craig Maier

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

29 minute listen

Forty iron rectangles, each one blunt as a piano key, rotate into a blurring fury that hides the eight-foot-long shaft at the heart of the flail chopper. I am perched atop several tons of iron, with 80 horsepower at my command. This part of farming is straightforward – even a mechanically challenged tree-hugger like me can manage to depress the clutch, shift into second, and ease the throttle forward. The tractor’s tall, deeply treaded tires churn, revolving into a smooth spin. Everything is spinning: fans, belts, alternator, the driveshaft, axles. I don’t understand the mechanism fully, yet the tractor and chopper and I are propelled forward across the knee-high whiskers of a coarsely bearded cornfield.

It is Indian summer in southern Wisconsin. My wife and I and our young son live here on her family’s farm. Both of us are employed off the farm, but on weekends and many evenings I am an apprentice to my father-in-law, David. Today, we are taking advantage of a brief period of warm, dry weather. Winter is approaching, and I could be spending the day beside our woodsplitter – the gasoline-sipping, hydraulically heroic mechanism that makes it possible to put up several cords of firewood quickly each year – but that work can wait until the cool, sunny days of fall are shoved aside by the relentless spin of the earth into darkness, sleet, snow and frozen ground.

The wall of tall green corn that stood here this summer has been transformed by fall and harvest. Little is standing after the field was stripped by a seed-combing combine. The mechanical tornado flails so loudly behind me: wailing against the air, grinding off the root-buttressed corn-stalk stumps, sucking up spent leaves and stripped cobs. In my wake, dry corn litter passes through the chopper like water compelled into frothy turbulence, falling again into an even, silent surface that hides so much activity below.

No time to waste – the weather is expected to hold for another day, and I need to cover the field before the light fails this afternoon. Tomorrow, David will rake this chewed-up detritus into windrows and then come back for another round to bale them up. While it is good to leave some of this thatch on the field – to keep a roof over the soil and guard against erosion by wind and rain – we can afford to borrow some of this, which also makes good straw. Wherever livestock are gathered in close quarters, their waste can produce concentrations of ammonia and other gases that can be harmful to animals and people alike. Adding straw slows the breakdown of manure and urine, reducing the production of noxious gases and suspending valuable nutrients in a semi-solid mixture. The straw and excrement will come back to this field loaded with nitrogen, phosphorous and other nutrients.

The ‘barn-pack’ is also heavy with organic matter that keeps a significant portion of the nutrients locked up for longer periods of time until it is broken down by the creatures who are at work beneath the calm surface of the field: literally tons of worms and beetles and other invertebrates; many miles of fungal hyphae; and countless diversity of bacteria. The denizens of this foodshed work to decompose the thick cell walls of the straw, as well as the partially digested grass stems and leaves that passed through the cattle and into their manure while the livestock fed on hay.

The creatures of the soil also feed on the bodies of the gut microbes that helped ruminants digest their hay. The gut-borne microbes are the true herbivores in this system: the power of the sun is harnessed by plants and turned into grain or hay, which is gathered by the farmers and transported to the barn, then delivered to the habitat of the gut by a large mammal whose brain, mouth and muscles spend their days gathering food for its microbial tenants. However, the microbes are short-lived and quickly finish their shift at the top of the system. As they die, they pass through the threshold of hind gut and, finally, the anus. Shit.

Is it fair to call any of this waste? The spark of life in the stinking barn pack is not yet exhausted, not yet lost to entropy. Roots burrow deep in search of more phosphorous, nitrogen and water to carry on the busy work of building ion transporters, enzymes, lignin and proteins – from root to stem to leaf to seed. Through spring, summer and fall, the straw, plant fibres and dead microbes that re-enter the field will take shifts in resurrection. Such is the life of the soil.

The end of the row breaks my reverie. I turn the tractor in a half-circle and feather the lever again until the tornado touches down just as I straighten out and catch the next row. Ready for another trip across the field, aimed down the rows, now due west. My route takes me just a few degrees north of where the late afternoon sun hangs in the soft yellow light of mid-latitude autumn.

I crest and ease on over oak-dappled ridges – glacial moraines – that attest to the furthest advance of the recent Ice Age glaciers and the fire-centric economy of the people who covered this land with effigy mounds and who later began to grow corn and other crops in fields they weeded using the shoulder blades of bison. Further west, a narrow, rusty-girdered bridge threads over the Mississippi River, carrying water that fell as rain and snow on north country forests, coulee pastures in the tri-state Driftless Area, and the broad, flat corn-and-soybean lands of central and western Minnesota. Each fall, the skies above fill with white pelicans, bald eagles and a paradise of waterfowl. Against this pattern of gathering and flow, I’d continue west, west: chopping through the dried stalks of compass plant and tall tassels of big bluestem at Hayden Prairie State Preserve in Iowa and fording the Big Sioux beneath the watch of yucca and side oats grama.

End of the row – decision time again.

Last September, I accompanied David to check out a field that lies due west of the stubble-chopping field, on the north bank of Prentice Creek. We were there to measure and mark a grass buffer that will separate row crops from the creek – a practice encoded in the conservation easement that is now a part of the deed to the property. Given the flash floods that have repeatedly swept across this low ground over the past few years, leaving this land in grass makes good economic and ecological sense. During the last major flood in 2008, David baled dusty hay from this field, while a substantial portion of his corn crop would have been completely lost. As we moved upstream to place more flags, I repeatedly plunged through the field-edge tangle of burdock, mulberry, eastern blackberry, woodland sunflowers and pointed-leaf tick-trefoil to find the eroded edge of the creek bank. It is not a pilgrim’s creek, but a real one, cut deep into topsoil that has eroded off the long-planted fields and into its dynamic basin. David planned to follow this line of flags a few days later, while spraying the rest of the old hayfield with glyphosate to kill the grass and alfalfa, and prepare for next spring’s planting of herbicide-resistant corn.

We spent an hour flagging the buffer, and the heat of the day was lapsing as we reached the property line. To get back to the truck, we followed a strip of weedy foxtail grasses that waved yellow seed heads in a rolling sea of hay. We were moving due west, as the foxtail marked precisely where the soil had been disturbed when David’s brother bulldozed the old fenceline a few years earlier. Halfway back to the truck, I was surprised when David stopped at a short, west-facing slope, where the field dropped about 10 feet over the course of 30-40 feet.

‘Let’s flag this, too,’ he said. Though I couldn’t see much of the soil beneath the late summer growth of alfalfa and grass, David said he knew the soil on this slope was light – a band of sand and gravel. Probably where an outwash stream trickled from the collapsing glacier. David pried up a few stones with his jackknife, and I turned over a few rounded and smooth stones in my hands. He quickly pointed out a pattern in the vegetation: ‘You can sort of see the change in soil in how the brome and alfalfa grows differently here. It’s thinner. This won’t be any good for corn, and it will erode away if the crop doesn’t take hold, so I’m going to leave it in hay. I’ll leave a broad-enough strip so I can come in from the buffer to bale it. The neighbours might laugh at me, but it’s the right thing to do.’

A land ethic cannot spring from the mind but must live, renew and evolve among families and communities

In that moment, I was an elated farm ecologist – I sensed that we shared a respect for the soil and a sense of responsibility to hold this ground. His decision could limit if not reverse soil erosion and perhaps build thicker topsoil, higher fertility and greater yields in the long run. In the short run, too, holding this ground with hay will be more profitable than buying seed, fertiliser and herbicide to plant hybrid corn. David uses all of those tools on his farm, yet they don’t drive all his farming decisions. He farms with a forethought that gives a fuller accounting of costs that come both out-of-pocket and at the expense of the health of the land.

Out in the field, he expressed his knowledge of the system and loyalty to the land through the language of conversation rather than the rhetoric of seminar or sermon. His knowledge was hard-won. He was now able to translate what he had observed in many a plough furrow to a subtle but discernible pattern in the field, which would otherwise appear as a uniform sea of green to the inattentive mind. He could make predictions, weigh costs and benefits, and chart a sustainable strategy without hardly pausing in his walk across the field. That kind of knowledge is not simply to be stored up, harboured and lost; it can be relayed along in the evolution of a locally adapted culture as he conveys, in situ, the knowledge to following generations.

With another year to add to my perspective, I have finally acknowledged what I could barely sense on that afternoon. My father-in-law was not talking to me as farmer to ecologist but as elder to apprentice. We agreed as professionals, but what was far more important than the congruence of our disciplined perspectives was the relationship we were building. When we choose to stay in place, we begin to feel the rub of constraints, responsibilities and uncertainties now placed on us by the past and future, while simultaneously the process provides opportunities for stronger human connections. There is within this a deep joy, satisfaction and hopefulness that is not readily available – perhaps not comprehensible – when we are in the process of pulling up stakes and heading out on the open road. The time I’ve spent learning to work on this farm has reinforced the idea that a land ethic cannot spring from the mind but must live, renew and evolve in the work and conversation that unfolds among families and communities.

Our antecedents derived the word ‘conversation’ from the Latin conversari. The root is also related to convertere, ‘to turn around’. On this level, conversation reflects the simple act of taking turns listening and speaking. Yet conversari itself meant ‘to live with or associate with’. Conversation, in this older sense, was more than just an exchange of words – it was an expression of shared life, of dwelling alongside one another in relationships of mutual dependence.

This ancient truth remains valid, even as the scale of our mutual turnings stretches far beyond family and village and watershed to encompass national and global communities through economic and cultural exchanges and the shared cycles of carbon and nitrogen, dust and pollution. No matter the distance that separates us, the lives of urban and rural people still turn around one another. An ethic grounded in this truth must be expressed in mutual interest in and concern for one another.

The goal of public policy for agriculture continues to be guided by the desire for cheap food

In the summer of 1947, the conservationist Aldo Leopold worked to integrate his thoughts on land use, weaving lands, wildness and ethics into a single essay, ‘The Land Ethic’, which became the capstone to his collection A Sand County Almanac (1949):

A land ethic, then, reflects the existence of an ecological conscience, and this in turn reflects a conviction of individual responsibility for the health of the land. Health is the capacity of the land for self-renewal. Conservation is our effort to understand and preserve this capacity.

The land ethic remains relevant in part because Leopold recognised his effort as a synthesis, as an articulation of the best of current understanding of people, land and the connections between them, rather than as the final word.

We still have far to go in the attempt to encode a land ethic sufficiently strong to temper our appetite for Earth’s resources and focus our work towards restoring land health. A land ethic, good land use, and an equitable and civil society arise from countless actions and conversations, constantly unfolding, as the nation’s citizens go about their daily lives.

Agriculture is an ecologically embedded enterprise, and we should not tolerate actions that degrade our natural capital, the diversity and function of our ecosystems, or the health of the atmosphere, soils and waters that surround and support us. At the same time, we must recognise that agriculture is embedded in society – a farm practice that runs counter to society’s goals is hard to maintain. I agree that a farm can and should be valued by its owners as a place to live, and as a source of pleasure in good farming, good eating and engagement with both domestic and wild neighbours. Society continues to measure farms, and judge farmers, on their production of grain, meat, biomass and other commodities. Farmers are caught up in a highly competitive market system that typically allows only a slim margin between money coming in and money going out. Meanwhile, the goal of public policy for agriculture continues to be guided by the desire for cheap food.

While the predicament of modern agriculture may appear so dire that we will inevitably adapt and organise a more sustainable system, ecologists at Murdoch University in Australia came to a different conclusion after analysing the problems facing farmers in the semi-arid southwestern part of that continent. Farmers and policy-makers continue to invest in production systems that don’t fit the land because they are now tightly bound up in patterns of modern agribusiness and food production. Financial capital goes to conventional farmers more easily than to alternative farmers, and social capital – in the forms of agronomic research, technical assistance (for addressing issues with animal health, soil fertility, soil erosion and water pollution), and especially processing, distribution and retail – supports the energy- and natural-capital intensive system. The authors describe this as a ‘lock-in trap’, ‘an industry that has so much “sunk-costs” that it may continue to degrade the resource it relies upon until the capital is totally removed.’ Shifting the system to a more desirable state – one that is ecologically as well as socially resilient – requires us to forge new social connections in the quest to establish more sustainable patterns of land use.

Can a community of well-connected but individually small actors hope to break agriculture out of its lock-in trap? There is little room for optimism, but our prospects are not hopeless. As David Orr reminds us: ‘Hope is a verb with its sleeves rolled up.’ When Orr encouraged us to be hopeful in times like these, perhaps he was continuing a literary conversation with Wendell Berry, a Kentucky hill country farmer and writer. Berry stated that he had no reason to be optimistic about the prospects of people becoming reconnected with the ‘wealth, health, knowledge, and pleasure of their country’, but still he concluded that ‘hope is one of our duties … The health of nature is the primary ground of hope – if we can find the humility and wisdom to accept nature as our teacher.’

We may have much to learn from how nature’s economy operates in the prairie. In the Flint Hills of Kansas, the prairies are truly dominated by tall grasses – big and small bluestem, switchgrass and Indiangrass account for around 80 per cent of the prairie’s windswept greenery. These grasses are so dominant because they are remarkably efficient. Unlike many other grasses, these species build channels in their leaves to make the process of photosynthesis more efficient than it is for their competitors. The grasses need comparatively fewer enzymes to carry out photosynthesis and thus require less nitrogen – a building block of enzymes. This is a major advantage, as the amount of nitrogen in the soil is often the limiting factor for plant growth – hence the artificial nitrogen we’re counselled to add to our gardens and crops as fertiliser. The tall grasses also lose less water thanks to their innovation, which helps put them ahead in dry climates with high evaporation rates.

In the language of microeconomics, the tall grasses have the lowest costs for construction and operations. As a result, these ships in the prairie sea can cast vast nets of roots below the surface to capture water and nitrogen, and set huge sails of green leaves to catch the sun to propel photosynthesis. These photons and molecules are finite resources that plants cannot share and for which they must compete. The highly efficient tallgrass fleets should rule the prairies. Paradoxically, the tallgrass prairies are blessed with an abundance of smaller, less efficient wildflowers and legumes, prospering from sub-boreal Manitoba in Canada to the subtropical coastal plains of Louisiana and Texas. As with the mystery of decay and renewal that abounds in the soil, microbes dwell at the heart of this paradox.

In the cycles of evolution, the efficiency and dominance of the tall grasses built a palace of greenery

All of us mammals have microbes in our guts, facilitating and regulating digestion. Large-bodied herbivores take this to an extreme – huge body cavities accommodate an intricate digestive system that shelters, feeds and harvests a community of microbes. Mouth, teeth, tongue, digestive tract and brain are all organised to harvest and process grass, leveraging the ability of microbes to consume the fibrous grasses and excrete easily digestible sugars.

In the tallgrass prairie, American bison select where to graze based, to some extent, on where they can maximise their intake of the plant resource to which they are best adapted. The ecological niche of an organism is perhaps most aptly translated as its palace, as the poet, translator and ecological activist Gary Snyder has re-discovered, and interpreted for us, in the work of the philosopher Dōgen. In the cycles of evolution, the efficiency and dominance of the tall grasses built a palace of greenery. The bison evolved to dwell in this palace. Among the tall grasses, they are fully at home.

As the ecologist Alan Knapp and his colleagues at Kansas State University digested from their research in the Flint Hills, the microbially facilitated bison play a key role in making their home a palace for others too. As they fulfil their needs by feasting on leaves, the bison demolish the tall grasses’ leafy superstructures. The rest of the prairie blushes and blooms in gratitude.

The leaves of big bluestem might otherwise have overshadowed a short-statured wild petunia seedling. Because the microbe/bison superorganism is adapted to make use of the abundant grass, the young wildflower now spends much of the summer bathed in light, taking in carbon dioxide, releasing oxygen, and building leaves and roots through photosynthesis. Furthermore, nitrogen in the big bluestem leaves would have been locked up through the rest of the growing season, unless a passing band of grasshoppers landed for a meal and carried it off, driven by the instinct to mate and lay eggs before the days become any shorter. As the bison eat and excrete, the nitrogen and other nutrients once held in the leaves overhead are returned in forms accessible to other community members. After pausing to scratch her belly on a compass plant, a bison cow returns a cascade of nitrogen-rich urine that the wildflower may absorb just as it begins to send its flowering stalk skyward.

The compass plant, in turn, could produce one more flower than it might have, had the nitrogen remained locked up in big bluestem. Its saucer-sized flowers attract and nourish many native pollinators, while its nutritious seeds are a staple for seed-eating birds. Both flowers and seeds are costly to produce because they concentrate large amounts of nitrogen. The compass plant and wild petunia are only two of hundreds of wildflower and grass species that can be outcompeted by the dominant tall grasses. When the bison home in on a patch of tall grasses, the dominance of the highly efficient big and small bluestem, Indiangrass and switchgrass may be depressed such that the prairie’s balance sheet might take a hit on the single measure of tons of biomass per acre – but, as Robinson Jeffers puts it in his poem ‘Bixby’s Landing’ (1928):

… what a good multitude
Is here in return …

In the process of reorganisation, exchange in other ecological currencies multiplies, for countless organisms dwell in the palace of wildflowers. Most herbivores and omnivores are smaller than a bison and lack the microbial symbiosis that provides access to grass. Instead, they depend upon the more digestible leaves, pollen, nectar, sugary fruit, starchy tubers and seeds, and protein-rich leaf buds that wildflowers and flowering shrubs produce. Badgers, rabbits, mice and voles, prairie chickens, grouse, turtles and waterfowl can all benefit. The less efficient plants host many species of insect larvae, which in turn feed predatory insects, songbird hatchlings and others on the food web. And so the web of connections rolls out and across the prairies in this fashion.

If we are to transform agriculture for better outcomes, we need a similar roll-out of networked and diverse people and organisations who collectively act as a keystone species. But we cannot simply wait for the bison of federal policy reform to come trampling through the industrial agriculture complex. We must act lest the bison of more sustainable agriculture stumble, allowing the most ruthless forces in industrial agriculture to continue unchecked – to the degradation of soil, extinction of wild plants and animals, and hollowing-out of communities. To restore agriculture to a more diverse and resilient community, each of us must express our individual land ethic through the food markets and by giving voice to our values in the public sphere. There are deep congruencies between sustainable agriculture and conservation, and we cannot afford to lose the incremental but crucial gains that pioneers have made over the past few decades.

Investing in local food and energy production creates demand for more types of agriculture, renewing ecological and social diversity across landscapes long simplified in the name of industrial efficiency. Such landscapes might include small, intensively cultivated vegetable fields and orchards supplying fresh produce and local processors; trellised hops adapted to local conditions and supporting regional breweries; perennial grasslands producing healthy animal products from cattle, sheep, swine and poultry; small fields of corn, wheat and other grains integrated with livestock or supplying locally owned mills; and oak woodlots thinned to provide firewood and lumber. Wetlands now choked with reed canarygrass and shrubs could once again support wildlife while providing hay, bedding and renewable biomass capable of heating homes, businesses and schools during winter’s deep freeze. By turning more of our dollars away from large agribusiness and toward these small-scale, locally integrated systems, we will be rewarded with healthier soil, cleaner and more abundant groundwater, fewer and less severe floods following intense rains, stronger communities with the skills to manage biologically complex farming systems, and a richer, more secure tapestry of semi-natural-to-wild habitats. Many semi-domestic parts of the rural landscape are important for the wild creatures that enrich our lives and testify to the care we take of the land. The touchstones of these partly wild/partly human landscapes are small pastures and sweeping grasslands, scattered woodlots and deep forests, shady valleys and sandstone-capped bluffs, clean headwater springs, and wetlands alive with waterfowl.

A diverse rural landscape, shaped by goals of complexity and resilience, rather than maximum production and minimal accounting, will be invaluable to our communities in the coming years. The landscape of diverse farming systems that rely much less on fossil fuels for energy and fertility is much more likely to remain productive despite shocks such as intense rains, flooding, drought, rising fuel and fertiliser costs, declining soil structure and fertility, and limited access to credit and financial capital. Such shocks are predicted to become more frequent and more severe because of climate change, continued population growth, increasing demand for resources, and economic and social inequality.

What could a large agribusiness, food-processing or cut-throat retail corporation fear more than for us to begin acting like we don’t believe there is much congruence between their sales and quarterly earnings, and our security and happiness? Berry has described such a social shift as nothing less than secession.

Love is at the heart of conservation, good farming and strong communities

Among the trade-offs that come with taking personal responsibility for investment in infrastructure and community is that much of the pay-off will come in the long term rather than in the next quarter or next few years. Building a long-term outlook and sustaining collective commitment will require cultivating the skills needed to navigate disagreements between individuals and factions, to face the uncertainty of alternative models of community development, to weather economic hard times, and to engage in both practical and joyful scepticism of the intense propaganda that flows from the anonymous economy to its victims. This demands vision, sincerity and the arts of neighbourliness and community engagement.

Nowhere in the frameworks of sustainability have I come across love for our neighbours and the land as a guiding principle, yet love is at the heart of conservation, good farming and strong communities. We do not know what the future will bring, but resilience to coming shocks cannot be secured through better technology, greater efficiency or improved communications infrastructure alone. We need all of these advances, but conservation asks even more of us. Leopold’s words resonated with this call when he summarised his goals for an ecological education:

If the individual has a warm personal understanding of land, he will perceive of his own accord that it is something more than a breadbasket. He will see land as a community of which he is only a member, albeit now the dominant one. He will see the beauty, as well as the utility, of the whole, and know the two cannot be separated. We love (and make intelligent use of) what we have learned to understand.

Each of us is an individual, but ecology and ecological economics remind us that we exist only in relation to the land and our neighbours. By enacting our love for the land and our neighbours, we assume great risk. We will likely face changes in consumption patterns and the nature of work and exchange that will feel like severe sacrifices. However, many rich harvests are indeed possible when we choose to act as members of our community, to transcend efficiency and strive toward harmony among people and between people and land. Much that might otherwise go to waste is brought back into cycles of renewal. As we nurture the life of community, we tend a field in which many of our hopes and pleasures can bloom.

End of row. Decision time again.

Craig Maier died in 2024. This essay has been lightly edited from his original manuscript for publication, with the guidance of Craig’s graduate advisor, Randy Jackson. With thanks to Randy for his valuable input in the editing process, and for helping to honour Craig’s memory.

item.title: How the West was fun
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
Be it movie mythos or nostalgia for a ‘simpler’ time, there’s an undeniable allure in stepping into the American West

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
‘Who wants a pistol? Raise your hand.’

At the Old Tucson theme park in Tucson, Arizona, visitors step out of their normal lives and into the city’s past. Or, more accurately, a funhouse mirror of the past that plays up the cowboy romance and tamps down the drudgery and poverty to cultivate a good ol’ time. Over the course of a day, the US directors Sue Ding and Sarah Garrahan capture visitors enjoying the park’s many attractions, including shooting games, live shows, rides and, of course, the opportunity to cosplay as sheriffs, outlaws and saloon girls in the old-timey photography studio. Throughout, park guests discuss what draws them to Old Tucson. Whether it’s movie mythos, a longing for a simpler, ‘less political’ era, or just the fun of escapism, there’s an undeniable allure in stepping into a romanticised past that never quite existed.

item.title: Toadstools and toxins
item.dc:creator: Eric Leas
item.description:
When I found the mushroom Amanita muscaria being sold in candy wrappers, I uncovered legal loopholes, dangerous dosages and more

- by Eric Leas

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

28 minute listen

In late summer 2023, I found myself in a smoke shop looking at a package of ‘magic mushroom’ gummies.

That phrase, magic mushrooms, usually calls to mind one type of mushroom: those containing psilocybin, the compound showing promise as a therapy for depression, addiction and other psychopathologies. But these gummies were not psilocybin. Instead, the packaging described Amanita muscaria, the red-capped, white-spotted toadstool of fairy-tale forests, iPhone keyboards and Super Mario.

I knew a little about the folklore of Amanita muscaria. I had first seen it discussed in an episode of the show Hamilton’s Pharmacopeia (2016-21), which begins with a claim I now hear often: that Amanita muscaria may be among the oldest human intoxicants. The New York banker-turned-ethnomycologist R Gordon Wasson, whose Life magazine essay from 1957 introduced psilocybin mushrooms to a mass Western audience, certainly took this idea seriously. In his book Soma: Divine Mushroom of Immortality (1968), he argued that the Vedic soma – a ritual drink in ancient Indian religions – was made from Amanita muscaria. The mushroom has also been linked, sometimes carefully and sometimes wildly, to the origins of Santa Claus, Viking berserkers and even Christianity. Some believe its other name, ‘fly agaric’, stems from its use as a natural pesticide for house flies; the word muscaria is also derived from the Latin word musca, meaning fly. Some scholars have linked Amanita muscaria to Lewis Carroll’s mushroom scene in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865), in which the Caterpillar tells Alice that ‘one side’ of the mushroom will make her taller and the other shorter, though Carroll does not identify a species.

But I wasn’t standing in that smoke shop holding one of these products as a folklorist or looking to lose myself in Carroll’s ‘golden afternoon’. I am a public-health scientist, and my questions were pragmatic: what exactly was in this package? Could it hurt someone? Were these products legal?

The first thing I did was what I usually do. I went to the scientific literature. And down the rabbit hole I tumbled.

Although manufacturers use the term ‘magic mushrooms’, the main psychoactive compound in Amanita muscaria is not pharmacologically interchangeable with psilocybin; the two drugs do not act on the brain in the same way.

The body converts psilocybin into psilocin, the substance that actually produces its psychedelic effects. Psilocin switches on serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, proteins on the surface of brain cells that respond to the chemical messenger serotonin. These receptors are concentrated in the cortex, the brain’s outer layer, and especially in the prefrontal cortex, the region behind the forehead involved in such functions as attention, perception and our sense of self. The receptors sit on the big output neurons that broadcast to the rest of the brain, and switching them on makes those cells fire harder. Brain scans of people on psilocybin show what follows: networks that normally run in step with each other come apart, and regions of the cortex that rarely signal to each other begin to. What people report from the inside is a change in perception rather than false perception – surfaces that appear to move, colours that intensify, time that stops running at a fixed rate.

Muscimol killed mice at a lower dose than nearly all psychotropic drugs we examined, including fentanyl

Amanita muscaria works through a different system. Its principal psychoactive compound, muscimol, acts primarily on GABA-A receptors – part of the brain’s main braking system – quieting neuronal activity rather than amping it up. That puts muscimol broadly on the inhibitory side of brain chemistry, the same signalling system influenced by central nervous system depressants such as benzodiazepines and alcohol. The experience is still ‘psychoactive’, but it can look quite different. Clinical reports of Amanita intoxication describe drowsiness and dream-like states, impaired balance and coordination, confusion and disorientation, sometimes alternating with agitation, as well as visual or auditory hallucinations. In severe cases, people can become profoundly sedated, delirious or lose consciousness. In other words, rather than the characteristic alterations in perception associated with psilocybin, Amanita can produce a much less orderly mixture of sedation, hallucination and confusion.

The risks are different too. When my colleagues and I began looking at the toxicology, the numbers startled me. By the crude measure toxicologists often begin with – the LD50, or the dose required to kill half the test population – published estimates suggested that muscimol administered orally killed mice at a lower dose than nearly all commonly used psychotropic drugs we examined, including fentanyl. As a vegetarian, I found the exercise grim, and translating animal doses to humans is always imperfect. But these were safety signals we took seriously.

That was the first turn in the rabbit hole. The next was dosing. If companies were selling Amanita muscaria gummies and chocolates in ordinary retail settings, then somewhere, implicitly or explicitly, someone had made a decision about dosing. A gummy contains some amount. A package contains some total amount. A label tells a consumer to take one piece, or half a piece, or perhaps more. A certificate of analysis from products submitted to a laboratory can provide an amount per gummy. Those numbers can feel reassuring simply because they are printed on a package. They also imply that someone knew enough to choose a dose for the desired effect.

I wanted to know whether that chain existed.

So, I started with a simple question: are there human studies showing what muscimol does at different doses? The best answer to this would have come from controlled studies in which multiple human participants were given standardised doses under observation, with careful reporting of effects and adverse events. I could not find that literature in the usual places. I could find toxicology estimates, case reports, historical accounts and ethnobotanical discussions. But a modern dosing study, the kind one would want before placing psychoactive candies near a cash register, was not there.

I kept looking.

Eventually, I came across the proceedings from a symposium I had not known about: the Ethnopharmacologic Search for Psychoactive Drugs, held at the University of California, San Francisco, from 28 to 30 January 1967. The time and place stood out to me immediately. Two weeks earlier, a couple of miles away in Golden Gate Park, Timothy Leary had told the Human Be-In crowd to ‘turn on, tune in, drop out’, a phrase that would become shorthand for the moral panic that soon surrounded psychedelics and particularly LSD. The symposium also opened with a letter by Albert Hofmann, the Swiss chemist best known for synthesising LSD and who had also led the work identifying psilocybin and psilocin as the active compounds of Psilocybe mexicana. The symposium covered compounds from many psychoactive plants and cultures, including a lecture on nutmeg delivered by Alexander Shulgin – the San Francisco Bay Area biochemist who is remembered most infamously (and perhaps unkindly) for his rediscovery and popularisation of MDMA (aka Ecstasy).

A mid-century scientist, dosing himself, may have produced numbers that later travelled into a marketplace of gummies

Near the end came a session on Amanita muscaria. In the final part of the final lecture, I found what I had been searching for – something resembling a dosing guide. It came from a report of a self-experiment with pure muscimol by Peter G Waser – a Swiss pharmacologist who later served as rector of the University of Zurich – under observation by a Swiss psychiatrist named Jules Angst. Waser repeatedly dosed himself with pure muscimol dissolved in water to establish a range of effects. This was not a modern dosing study. It was stranger than that, and I think it is worth hearing Waser’s language directly because it captures both the scientific seriousness and the unease of the moment:

Curiosity is one of the main qualities of a scientist, and this may be the reason why a pharmacologist watching the behaviour of his animals under certain drugs wants to know more about the emotions and changes in reaction they produce. Another reason is ethical. We have to foresee the accidents and dangerous actions new compounds of general interest may produce on man. My report on some experiments done on myself by ingesting ibotenic acid and muscimol under careful psychiatric control may give you an unauthoritative view on this.

At 5 milligrams taken orally in water, Waser reported little effect beyond a feeling of laziness. At 10 milligrams, however, he described a mild intoxication beginning about 90 minutes later, with dizziness, loss of coordination and elevated mood. He did not experience hallucinations, although he noticed slight changes in taste and colour vision, followed by muscle twitching and then sleep with dreams. Within two to three hours, he reported feeling normal again – rested and able to work – and said he slept deeply the following night.

At 15 milligrams, the effects were stronger and began more quickly, after about 40 minutes. Waser reported dizziness severe enough that he could not walk with his eyes closed, along with slurred speech, diminished appetite and taste, and increasing difficulty concentrating. His visual perception also changed: images of situations he had seen minutes earlier seemed to repeat themselves, and sounds sometimes appeared to echo. Most disturbing to him were repeated involuntary muscle contractions. At times, he wrote, he felt as though he had lost his legs, although he specifically distinguished the experience from the vivid, colourful hallucinations he had experienced with LSD. After falling asleep and awakening several hours later, he felt dull and uncertain rather than refreshed, although the muscle twitching had diminished. His blood pressure rose only slightly during the psychoactive period. In preliminary analyses conducted by the Swiss chemist Conrad H Eugster, muscimol appeared to be detectable in Waser’s urine after the self-experiment, although Waser cautioned, at the time, that the finding still needed confirmation.

What I found was upsetting, but not that surprising. Dosing recommendations from product manufacturers, including the one I found at that smoke shop, appeared to resemble that old self-experiment. While I have no way to confirm it, I have a strange feeling that this mid-century scientist, dosing himself under observation and reporting on it at a famous drug conference, may have produced numbers that later travelled into a marketplace of gummies and chocolates sold to consumers who likely have no idea where the guidance came from.

I wish I had been able to speak with Waser himself, but he died in 2010. In 2024, I did exchange emails with Angst, the psychiatrist who had supervised the experiment. Angst was 97 and not in good health, but he confirmed the point that mattered most to me: Waser had come to Angst for supervision as a precaution. Waser’s own later writing suggests why. Recalling the experiments, Waser described the experiences at high doses as unpleasant and even potentially life-threatening.

Convinced of questionable dosing standards in this marketplace, my line of enquiry returned to the potential harms – were there products on the market that contained enough muscimol to seriously harm someone?

I found a product with a very high reported amount of muscimol. It was a gummy product, one in a benign-looking package that did not have childproofing or clear warnings. I began doing the calculation no one wants to do. If a young child ate the entire package, mistaking it for candy, could they die? I took the reported amount of muscimol, the toxicology estimates (the LD50), a conversion used to translate dosing between species, and the average weight of a small child. The result looked bad. Bad enough that I did not quite trust myself. So, I called a friend, Matthieu Rouffet, a medicinal chemist and the dean of science at a local college, who does toxicology calculations more often than I do. I wanted him to tell me I had made an error. Instead, he was alarmed too.

There is a rare moment as a scientist when you encounter an empirical finding and it becomes emotionally charged. Before, it might just have been intellectual curiosity and your training that drove you to it. After, you feel a sense of responsibility. This was one of those rare moments for me. Perhaps this finding was especially emotionally charged for my friend Matthieu and me because we are fathers of young children. When I made the calculation, my daughter was only a year old. It could have just been the sleep-deprived delirium of early fatherhood, but I felt a moral responsibility to act.

The broader pattern appeared to be permissiveness by omission or legal loophole

Were there policy levers I could pull? It was complex because Amanita muscaria fell into the gap between the categories – not a controlled substance, not a food, not quite a supplement.

Unlike psilocybin, Amanita muscaria and muscimol were not scheduled under the US Controlled Substances Act, and they also did not appear to be controlled under comparable drug laws in most countries, with a few exceptions. The Netherlands treated Amanita muscaria and Amanita pantherina (which also contains muscimol) as controlled substances, and, in the US, manufacturers generally acknowledged Louisiana as a state where sales were restricted. One manufacturer’s legal guidance listed prohibitions in countries including Brazil, Thailand, Australia, Romania, Russia, Sweden and Ukraine. But the broader pattern appeared to be permissiveness by omission or legal loophole.

This was an argument I had seen a few years earlier, when I wrote about the ‘hemp loophole’. It emerged from the 2018 Farm Bill legalising hemp, defined largely by its low level of delta-9-THC, the main intoxicant in cannabis. Some manufacturers saw an opening: if the law restricted just delta-9-THC, they argued, other intoxicating cannabinoids derived from legal hemp could still be sold. One was delta-8-THC, often produced from hemp-derived CBD, a nonintoxicating cannabinoid. Soon delta-8 gummies, vapes and candies were turning up in gas stations, smoke shops and online stores. The industry’s argument was essentially this: if the starting material was legal hemp and the finished product stayed below the federal limit for delta-9-THC, it did not have to be sold through the regulated marijuana market, with safeguards such as age restrictions and testing for potency.

The Amanita muscaria market seemed to be borrowing a similar playbook. The claim was not that Amanita muscaria gummies had been proven safe. It was that they were not psilocybin, not scheduled, and not clearly prohibited.

However, drug scheduling was only one possible policy lever. Food and dietary supplement law was another. Many Amanita muscaria products were being sold as if they were ordinary foods or supplements, but I could not find publicly available notifications showing that Amanita muscaria or muscimol had been accepted as a new dietary ingredient in the US or elsewhere.

Regulators could clarify whether these products could be commercially manufactured and sold at all

Given the toxicology and case reports mentioned above, that absence mattered. The issue, here, was not whether someone could pick a mushroom in the woods and take it home to eat – that’s unambiguously legal. The issue was whether a company could extract, concentrate, flavour, package, advertise, and sell a psychoactive compound in candy-like forms without meeting basic consumer protection standards.

They didn’t appear to be meeting this standard, and so there was legal recourse. Regulators could clarify whether these products could be commercially manufactured and sold at all under dietary supplement and food laws. If sales were not allowed, they could take the products off the shelves. If sales were allowed, they could require product standards such as age restrictions, child-resistant packaging, maximum-dose rules, warning labels, restrictions on cartoons or candy-like marketing, and standardised testing for potency, contaminants and undisclosed drugs. They could also require labels to state what was in the package in units that were interpretable.

Now, with a clear safety concern and a clear pathway for legal recourse, my colleagues and I wrote a paper, published in a peer-reviewed journal, and we began raising awareness on the subject. I issued a press release with my school at the University of California, San Diego, which helped to generate some national media coverage including in The Washington Post and on NPR. I also contacted colleagues at the Department of Justice in my home state of California. They put me in touch with the consumer-safety division that would eventually build an investigation of several brands selling Amanita muscaria-branded products in the state, including one that led to the seizure of more than 95,000 mushroom chocolate bars from a warehouse in San Diego County.

By late 2024, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had also reached its own conclusion about Amanita muscaria in food, offering a perspective that confirmed my own. In a scientific memorandum, FDA toxicologists concluded that Amanita muscaria and three of its active constituents, including muscimol, do not meet the criteria for safe use in food in the US.

There’s another side to the story. Some people believe the mushroom helps them. There are books and online communities organised around microdosing Amanita muscaria, often motivated by purported benefits based on, and following dosing information derived from, survey responses or anecdotal reports. The health claims tend to cluster around sleep, anxiety and the possibility of reducing dependence on benzodiazepines or other sedatives. Muscimol’s pharmacology makes some of this plausible in a broad mechanistic sense. A compound acting primarily on the GABA-A receptors could, in theory, have sedating effects that are therapeutic. Even our forerunner Waser alludes to this in his self-experiment. That account also mentions the findings of his colleague Eugster, who held a patent on a method of synthesising muscimol, which is currently assigned to the pharmaceutical company Novartis. Less toxic analogues of muscimol have also been explored as pharmaceuticals; gaboxadol, for instance, was discovered by the Danish chemist Povl Krogsgaard-Larsen. But the benefits and harms of these substances have never been rigorously tested to this day.

A thousand testimonials about the use of Amanita muscaria do not tell you what is in a gummy from a particular batch made by a particular company. They do not establish a safe range for children, older adults, pregnant people, people taking other medications, or anyone who eats more than the label recommends because the product looks harmless.

Once a substance is turned into a consumer good, science and capitalism are already in the room

This is one of the tensions running through the modern conversation about psychedelics and plant medicines like Amanita muscaria. Some proponents of plant medicine argue that science should not be treated as the only legitimate way of evaluating the veracity of therapeutic claims. They point to traditional and Indigenous uses of psychoactive plants and fungi, sometimes over millennia, and ask why randomised controlled trials should outrank lived experience, ritual knowledge or community practice.

I take that argument seriously. Western medicine does not own all wisdom, and therapeutic approval pathways are limited. Many plant medicines will struggle through conventional drug approval because they cannot be easily patented, because no company has an incentive to fund the studies, or because they belong in a ceremonial setting that is not transferable to a randomised trial. If the only knowledge we recognise is knowledge that can be monetised through drug development, we will miss a great deal.

But the Amanita muscaria products sold in smoke shops are not simply traditional plant medicines being used in traditional contexts. They are commercial products in a modern marketplace. They are manufactured, packaged, branded, advertised, and shipped. They borrow the language of science, from microdosing to certificates of analysis, when it helps them. Once a substance is turned into a consumer good, science and capitalism are already in the room. The question is whether they will be used with integrity.

The distinction between plant medicine and a commercial market became painfully clear with the recall of Diamond Shruumz-brand chocolate bars, ice-cream cones and gummies sold by Prophet Premium Blends, based in Santa Ana, California. In 2024, federal agencies investigated 180 cases, including three potential deaths, tied to products marketed with mushroom language and sold in the same broad retail ecosystem of gas stations, smoke shops, hemp-derived cannabinoid stores and online sellers.

In their recall notice, Prophet Premium Blends indicated that the adverse events may have been due to elevated levels of muscimol. But product testing complicated that story. Muscimol did not appear in all products and could not explain all the reported symptoms. Instead, testing found a shifting mixture of substances across products, including psilacetin, a near chemical cousin of psilocin first disclosed in a patent by Albert Hofmann and Franz Troxler in 1961. Unlike psilocin and psilocybin, psilacetin is not always listed by name in controlled-substance schedules, though it may still be regulated under analogue laws or broader drug-control provisions. Some samples also contained psilocin, pregabalin (a prescription medication), and compounds related to the psychoactive root, kava. The result was not a simple story about muscimol toxicity. It was a more troubling story about a marketplace where consumers could not reliably know what psychoactive substances they were consuming.

That, to me, illustrates the central ethical issue I see in the conversation about modern psychedelics and plant medicines.

People can argue about whether adults should be allowed to use psychedelics or plant medicines. My own view is that adults should generally have wide latitude over what they put in their own bodies. But they also have a right to know what they are putting in their bodies, as well as the known benefits and risks. A person cannot meaningfully consent to ingesting one thing while being sold another. They cannot weigh risks that are hidden from them inside of mislabelled gummies. They cannot dose carefully when the dose is uncertain and the active ingredient is undisclosed. The right to alter one’s consciousness does not include a company’s right to deceive.

Psilocybin was creating a halo around other mushrooms, and manufacturers were exploiting it

And while there are many stories about the purported benefits of plant medicines like Amanita muscaria, there are also stories about the harms of this marketplace. The most impactful story I’ve learned about came from Ashley Glover, who contacted me through email in 2024.

Ashley first wrote to me after reading my peer-reviewed article. Her only brother Andrew Davenport died on 23 June 2024, she said, after consuming a Diamond Shruumz mushroom bar. What stood out in Ashley’s emails was not only the grief, but the difficulty of getting the justice system to recognise what might have happened. She wrote that a witness who was with Andrew had insisted that the bars made him sick. She wrote that an opened box of Diamond Shruumz bars was recovered near his body. She also wrote that his initial toxicology report did not show hard drugs or alcohol, and that his prescribed medications were described to the family as being at normal therapeutic levels. But the medical examiner, she said, had not saved the box or bars for testing and the explanation relayed to her was blunt: no one overdoses on magic mushrooms.

That sentence has stayed with me because it captures the potential danger of a category error. If the product had been treated as a psilocybin mushroom, its risk could be dismissed before the relevant chemistry was even known. But these products were not psilocybin mushrooms. They were manufactured psychoactive goods whose contents could vary, whose labels could be incomplete, and whose compounds were difficult for forensic scientists to detect.

Ashley told me that biological samples from Andrew were eventually sent for specialised testing. Whether those results can establish causation is a legal and forensic question, and I do not want to claim more than the evidence can support. But her account shows the public-health problem in human terms. Once a consumer product enters the marketplace without reliable safety evidence, accurate labelling and adequate testing capacity, the uncertainty does not end at the point of sale. It follows the consumer, the family, the medical examiner, the investigator, and anyone trying to reconstruct what happened after an adverse event leaves questions in its wake.

I began this investigation with a question that seemed narrow enough for an academic paper – should unregulated sales of Amanita muscaria products prompt a public-health response? The answer, to me, became an unequivocal yes. But the journey was stranger than the paper could contain.

I did not set out to become the public-health scientist warning people about the fairy-tale mushroom, sounding alarmist or like a teetotaller. I am not opposed to research on psychoactive substances or to responsible use among adults. If anything, the therapeutic promise of psilocybin is part of why Amanita muscaria bothered me; psilocybin was creating a halo around other mushrooms, and manufacturers were exploiting it in ways that I saw as unethical and dangerous.

The lesson I took from Amanita muscaria was not that altered states are inherently dangerous or that science should flatten every human encounter with plants or fungus into a risk calculation. It was simpler than that. If a company sells a psychoactive product to the public, especially in forms that look like candy, it should be transparent about what is in the product, and have evidence that the product can be used without unreasonable harm. This should not be a radical standard. It should be the minimum requirement for sales.
